sets.title: Dance finalists and composers
sets.contentHtml:
Princess, Queen, Rani and Samragni were the four finalists in a dance competition. Ashman, Badal, Gagan and Dyu were the four music composers who individually assigned items to the dancers. Each dancer had to individually perform in two dance items assigned by the different composers. The first items performed by the four dancers were all assigned by different music composers. No dancer performed her second item before the performance of the first item by any other dancers. The dancers performed their second items in the same sequence of their performance of their first items.

The following additional facts are known.

  1. No composer who assigned item to Princess, assigned any item to Queen.
  2. No composer who assigned item to Rani, assigned any item to Samragni.
  3. The first performance was by Princess; this item was assigned by Badal.
  4. The last performance was by Rani; this item was assigned by Gagan.
  5. The items assigned by Ashman were performed consecutively. The number of performances between items assigned by each of the remaining composers was the same.

sets.title: Game show prize boxes
sets.contentHtml: A new game show on TV has 100 boxes numbered 1, 2, . . . , 100 in a row, each containing a mystery prize. The prizes are items of different types, a, b, c, . . . , in decreasing order of value. The most expensive item is of type a, a diamond ring, and there is exactly one of these. You are told that the number of items at least doubles as you move to the next type. For example, there would be at least twice as many items of type b as of type a, at least twice as many items of type c as of type b and so on. There is no particular order in which the prizes are placed in the boxes.

sets.title: Supermarket shelves
sets.contentHtml:
A supermarket has to place 12 items (coded A to L) in shelves numbered 1 to 16. Five of these items are types of biscuits, three are types of candies and the rest are types of savouries. Only one item can be kept in a shelf. Items are to be placed such that all items of same type are clustered together with no empty shelf between items of the same type and at least one empty shelf between two different types of items. At most two empty shelves can have consecutive numbers.

The following additional facts are known.

  1. A and B are to be placed in consecutively numbered shelves in increasing order.
  2. I and J are to be placed in consecutively numbered shelves both higher numbered than the shelves in which A and B are kept.
  3. D, E and F are savouries and are to be placed in consecutively numbered shelves in increasing order after all the biscuits and candies.
  4. K is to be placed in shelf number 16.
  5. L and J are items of the same type, while H is an item of a different type.
  6. C is a candy and is to be placed in a shelf preceded by two empty shelves.
  7. L is to be placed in a shelf preceded by exactly one empty shelf.

sets.title: Street map lines of sight
sets.contentHtml:
The figure below shows the street map for a certain region with the street intersections marked from a through l. A person standing at an intersection can see along straight lines to other intersections that are in her line of sight and all other people standing at these intersections. For example, a person standing at intersection g can see all people standing at intersections b, c, e, f, h, and k. In particular, the person standing at intersection g can see the person standing at intersection e irrespective of whether there is a person standing at intersection f.

Six people U, V, W, X, Y, and Z, are standing at different intersections. No two people are standing at the same intersection.

The following additional facts are known.

  1. X, U, and Z are standing at the three corners of a triangle formed by three street segments.
  2. X can see only U and Z.
  3. Y can see only U and W.
  4. U sees V standing in the next intersection behind Z.
  5. W cannot see V or Z.
  6. No one among the six is standing at intersection d.

sets.title: Archery tournament
sets.contentHtml:
Six players – Tanzi, Umeza, Wangdu, Xyla, Yonita and Zeneca competed in an archery tournament. The tournament had three compulsory rounds, Rounds 1 to 3. In each round every player shot an arrow at a target. Hitting the centre of the target (called bull’s eye) fetched the highest score of 5. The only other possible scores that a player could achieve were 4, 3, 2 and 1. Every bull’s eye score in the first three rounds gave a player one additional chance to shoot in the bonus rounds, Rounds 4 to 6. The possible scores in Rounds 4 to 6 were identical to the first three.

A player’s total score in the tournament was the sum of his/her scores in all rounds played by him/her. The table below presents partial information on points scored by the players after completion of the tournament. In the table, NP means that the player did not participate in that round, while a hyphen means that the player participated in that round and the score information is missing.

Tanzi-4-5NPNP

The following facts are also known.

  1. Tanzi, Umeza and Yonita had the same total score.
  2. Total scores for all players, except one, were in multiples of three.
  3. The highest total score was one more than double of the lowest total score.
  4. The number of players hitting bull’s eye in Round 2 was double of that in Round 3.
  5. Tanzi and Zeneca had the same score in Round 1 but different scores in Round 3.

sets.title: Vendor evaluation radar chart
sets.contentHtml: Five vendors are being considered for a service. The evaluation committee evaluated each vendor on six aspects – Cost, Customer Service, Features, Quality, Reach, and Reliability. Each of these evaluations are on a scale of 0 (worst) to 100 (perfect). The evaluation scores on these aspects are shown in the radar chart. For example, Vendor 1 obtains a score of 52 on Reliability, Vendor 2 obtains a score of 45 on Features and Vendor 3 obtains a score of 90 on Cost.

questions.stemHtml: Which digit does the letter A represent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Decoding the sum (columns from the right):

  • Units: F + F ends in F, so F = 0 with no carry.
  • Hundred-thousands: H + H + carry ends in F = 0. H ≠ 0, so 2H + carry = 10, giving H = 5, with no carry into that column and a carry of 1 out of it.
  • The sum has 7 digits, so its leading A is the final carry: A = 1. Then B + A + 1 = 1 + 10 gives B = 9.
  • Hundreds: A + F + c = C, i.e. 1 + c = C with C ≠ 1, so the tens column carries 1 and C = 2.
  • Tens: G + K = 1 + 10 = 11. Thousands: A + J = G with no carry, so G = J + 1.

The remaining digits 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 go to D, E, G, J, K. G = J + 1 and G + K = 11 allow (G, J, K) = (4, 3, 7), (7, 6, 4) or (8, 7, 3). D and E take the two leftover digits: {6, 8}, {3, 8} or {4, 6}.

So A = 1.

questions.stemHtml: Which among the digits 3, 4, 6 and 7 cannot be represented by the letter D?
questions.solutionHtml:
Decoding the sum (columns from the right):

  • Units: F + F ends in F, so F = 0 with no carry.
  • Hundred-thousands: H + H + carry ends in F = 0. H ≠ 0, so 2H + carry = 10, giving H = 5, with no carry into that column and a carry of 1 out of it.
  • The sum has 7 digits, so its leading A is the final carry: A = 1. Then B + A + 1 = 1 + 10 gives B = 9.
  • Hundreds: A + F + c = C, i.e. 1 + c = C with C ≠ 1, so the tens column carries 1 and C = 2.
  • Tens: G + K = 1 + 10 = 11. Thousands: A + J = G with no carry, so G = J + 1.

The remaining digits 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 go to D, E, G, J, K. G = J + 1 and G + K = 11 allow (G, J, K) = (4, 3, 7), (7, 6, 4) or (8, 7, 3). D and E take the two leftover digits: {6, 8}, {3, 8} or {4, 6}.

D can be 6 or 8 (first case), 3 or 8 (second) or 4 or 6 (third). 7 is always used by K, G or J, so D can never be 7.

questions.stemHtml: Which among the digits 4, 6, 7 and 8 cannot be represented by the letter G?
questions.solutionHtml:
Decoding the sum (columns from the right):

  • Units: F + F ends in F, so F = 0 with no carry.
  • Hundred-thousands: H + H + carry ends in F = 0. H ≠ 0, so 2H + carry = 10, giving H = 5, with no carry into that column and a carry of 1 out of it.
  • The sum has 7 digits, so its leading A is the final carry: A = 1. Then B + A + 1 = 1 + 10 gives B = 9.
  • Hundreds: A + F + c = C, i.e. 1 + c = C with C ≠ 1, so the tens column carries 1 and C = 2.
  • Tens: G + K = 1 + 10 = 11. Thousands: A + J = G with no carry, so G = J + 1.

The remaining digits 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 go to D, E, G, J, K. G = J + 1 and G + K = 11 allow (G, J, K) = (4, 3, 7), (7, 6, 4) or (8, 7, 3). D and E take the two leftover digits: {6, 8}, {3, 8} or {4, 6}.

G can be 4, 7 or 8. G = 6 would need J = 5, which is H's digit, so G cannot be 6.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true?

options.textHtml: The third performance was composed by Ashman
The second performance was composed by Dyu.
The second performance was composed by Gagan
The third performance was composed by Dyu

questions.solutionHtml:
Key deductions. All first items come before any second item, so performances 1–4 are first items and 5–8 are second items in the same dancer order. Princess is 1st and Rani's last item is 8th, so Rani is 4th: the order is P, ?, ?, R, P, ?, ?, R.

Performances 1–4 use four different composers, and Princess and Queen share none (likewise Rani and Samragni), so each composer has exactly two items, one among 1–4 and one among 5–8. Ashman's items are consecutive, so they must be 4 and 5: Rani (first) and Princess (second). Hence Princess = Badal, Ashman; Queen = Gagan, Dyu; Rani = Ashman, Gagan; Samragni = Badal, Dyu.

Trying the orders P-Q-S-R and P-S-Q-R, only P-S-Q-R gives Badal, Gagan and Dyu the same gap (4):

Performance12345678
DancerPrincessSamragniQueenRaniPrincessSamragniQueenRani
ComposerBadalDyuGaganAshmanAshmanBadalDyuGagan

The 2nd performance (Samragni) was composed by Dyu: B.

questions.stemHtml: What is the minimum possible number of different types of prizes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Set-up: there is exactly 1 item of type a, each later type has at least double the previous count, and all 100 boxes are filled, so the counts add up to 100.

One type cannot fill 100 boxes because type a has only 1 item. Two types work: 1 + 99 (99 ≥ 2). Minimum = 2.

questions.stemHtml: What is the maximum possible number of different types of prizes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Set-up: there is exactly 1 item of type a, each later type has at least double the previous count, and all 100 boxes are filled, so the counts add up to 100.

The smallest totals for k types are 1, 1+2, …, 1+2+4+8+16+32 = 63 for 6 types, and 127 for 7 types, which is more than 100. Six types work: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 69. Maximum = 6.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is not possible?

options.textHtml: There are exactly 60 items of type d.
There are exactly 30 items of type b
There are exactly 45 items of type c
There are exactly 75 items of type e

questions.solutionHtml:
Set-up: there is exactly 1 item of type a, each later type has at least double the previous count, and all 100 boxes are filled, so the counts add up to 100.

Test each option:

  • d = 60: 1 + 9 + 30 + 60 = 100 works (9 ≥ 2, 30 ≥ 18, 60 ≥ 60).
  • b = 30: 1 + 30 + 69 = 100 works.
  • c = 45: a type after c would need at least 90 items, too many, so c is the last type and b = 100 − 1 − 45 = 54. But c ≥ 2b would need b ≤ 22. Not possible.
  • e = 75: 1 + 2 + 4 + 18 + 75 = 100 works.

Answer: C.

questions.stemHtml: You ask for the type of item in box 45. Instead of being given a direct answer, you are told that there are 31 items of the same type as box 45 in boxes 1 to 44 and 43 items of the same type as box 45 in boxes 46 to 100. What is the maximum possible number of different types of items?
questions.solutionHtml:
Set-up: there is exactly 1 item of type a, each later type has at least double the previous count, and all 100 boxes are filled, so the counts add up to 100.

Box 45's type has 31 + 1 + 43 = 75 items. A later type would need at least 150 items, so this is the last type, and the other types share 100 − 75 = 25 items.

Four earlier types need at least 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 ≤ 25, for example 1, 2, 4, 18, then 75 (75 ≥ 36). Five earlier types need at least 31 > 25. So the maximum is 4 + 1 = 5: D.

questions.stemHtml: In how many different ways can the items be arranged on the shelves?
questions.solutionHtml:
Key deductions. There are 12 items and 4 empty shelves. Savouries come after biscuits and candies, and K is on shelf 16, so K is a savoury and the savoury block is D13, E14, F15, K16. Shelf 12 must be empty. Shelves 1–11 hold 5 biscuits, 3 candies and 3 empty shelves, with at most 2 consecutive empties, so at most 1 empty sits just before shelf 12.

C (a candy) starts its block after two empty shelves, and L starts the other block after exactly one empty shelf. Two layouts are possible:

  • Case 1: empty 1, 2; candies 3–5 with C at 3; empty 6; biscuits 7–11 with L at 7; empty 12. H must differ in type from L, so H is a candy. A, B, I, J are biscuits: L7, A8, B9, I/J at 10–11. G and H take 4–5.
  • Case 2: empty 1; biscuits 2–6 with L at 2; empty 7, 8; candies 9–11 with C at 9; empty 12. J is a biscuit, and I, adjacent to J, is too. A and B lie below I and J, so L2, A3, B4, I/J at 5–6. Candies are C9 plus G and H at 10–11.

In each case I/J can swap and G/H can swap, giving 4 arrangements per case.

Total = 4 + 4 = 8: D.

questions.stemHtml: Who is standing at intersection a?
questions.solutionHtml:
Key deductions. The only triangles made of three street segments are b-c-g and b-f-g, both using the diagonal b-g. U, Z, V lie on one line with V at the next intersection beyond Z. Testing every placement of U and Z on these triangles:

  • Lines through d, or lines that end at g or b, leave no place for V. Placements with X at g leave Y with no spot that sees only U and W.
  • The only placement that works is X = b, U = g, Z = f, V = e (g → f → e). X at b sees a, c, d, f, g, j, so a, c, d and j are empty.
  • Y must see U (g) but not X, V or Z, so Y = k. W is then on k's column, at i or l. i sees e (V), so W = l.

Final: X b, Z f, U g, V e, Y k, W l. Intersections a, c, d, h, i, j are empty.

Nobody is at a: A.

V at e sees along column e-f-g-h (Z, U) and row a-e-i (both empty). V sees U and Z only: C.

questions.stemHtml: What is the minimum number of street segments that X must cross to reach Y?
questions.solutionHtml:
Key deductions. The only triangles made of three street segments are b-c-g and b-f-g, both using the diagonal b-g. U, Z, V lie on one line with V at the next intersection beyond Z. Testing every placement of U and Z on these triangles:

  • The only placement that works is X = b, U = g, Z = f, V = e (g → f → e). X at b sees a, c, d, f, g, j, so a, c, d and j are empty.
  • Y must see U (g) but not X, V or Z, so Y = k. W is then on k's column, at i or l. i sees e (V), so W = l.

Final: X b, Z f, U g, V e, Y k, W l. Intersections a, c, d, h, i, j are empty.

X at b reaches Y at k by b → g (the diagonal) → k: 2 segments. No single segment joins b to k. Answer: D.

questions.stemHtml: Should a new person stand at intersection d, who among the six would she see?
questions.solutionHtml:
Key deductions. The only triangles made of three street segments are b-c-g and b-f-g, both using the diagonal b-g. U, Z, V lie on one line with V at the next intersection beyond Z. Testing every placement of U and Z on these triangles:

  • Lines through d, or lines that end at g or b, leave no place for V. Placements with X at g leave Y with no spot that sees only U and W.
  • The only placement that works is X = b, U = g, Z = f, V = e (g → f → e). X at b sees a, c, d, f, g, j, so a, c, d and j are empty.
  • Y must see U (g) but not X, V or Z, so Y = k. W is then on k's column, at i or l. i sees e (V), so W = l.

Final: X b, Z f, U g, V e, Y k, W l. Intersections a, c, d, h, i, j are empty.

From d she sees column a-b-c (X at b) and row h-l (W at l): W and X only, C.

questions.stemHtml: What was the highest total score?
questions.solutionHtml:
Key deductions. The number of bonus rounds a player shot equals their bull's eyes in Rounds 1–3. Tanzi has 1, Umeza 2, Wangdu 0, Xyla 3 (5, 5, 5), Yonita 1 and Zeneca 2.

  • Possible totals: Tanzi 14 + t (15–18), Umeza 13 + u (14–17), Yonita 13 + y (14–17). These three are equal. If their common total were not a multiple of 3, three players would break fact 2, so the total is 15: Tanzi's non-bull score is 1, Umeza's is 2 and Yonita's is 2.
  • Fact 5: if Tanzi's R1 were 1, Zeneca's R1 would be 1 too, putting Zeneca's 5s in R2 and R3, the same R3 as Tanzi. So Tanzi = 5, 4, 1 and Zeneca's R1 = 5, with R3 ≠ 1.
  • Fact 4: Xyla always hits in R2 and R3. If only Xyla hit in R3, Umeza and Zeneca would both hit in R1 and R2, making R2's count at least 3, not 2. So R3 has 2 hits and R2 has 4 (Xyla, Umeza, Yonita, Zeneca). Umeza = 2, 5, 5. Zeneca = 5, 5, z with z ≠ 5 and z ≠ 1. Yonita = 2, 5, 3.
  • Totals: Zeneca = 20 + z (22–24), Xyla = 21 + R6 (22–26), Wangdu = 4 + R1 + R3 (6–12, the lowest). Fact 3 makes the highest score 2W + 1. If W were a multiple of 3, the highest would be 13, 19 or 25, so 25 with W = 12. If W were not, only W = 7 or 10 keep the counts in fact 2 consistent, giving a highest of 15 or 21, below Zeneca's minimum of 22. So W = 12, highest = 25 = Xyla (the one non-multiple of 3), and Zeneca's total is a multiple of 3, i.e. 24.

Totals: Tanzi 15, Umeza 15, Yonita 15, Wangdu 12, Zeneca 24, Xyla 25.

Highest = 25 (Xyla): A.
